items.title: The Glorious Revolution was a Dutch invasion
items.claim: William of Orange landed in Devon on 5 November 1688. How large was the force?

options.text: A diplomatic mission of a few hundred men
Around 15,000 troops on 463 ships — larger than the Spanish Armada
Only James II's English defectors, no foreign troops
A small English army recruited in advance by Parliament

items.reveal:
Seven English nobles (the 'Immortal Seven') invited William in June 1688. He landed at Brixham, Devon, with 15,000-21,000 Dutch troops, plus thousands of horses and 50 cannon. James II's army melted; key officers (including John Churchill, the future Duke of Marlborough) defected.

James fled to France in December. The Convention Parliament (January 1689) declared the throne vacant and offered it to William and Mary. The Bill of Rights followed in December 1689.

The Williamite War in Ireland (Boyne 1690) and the Highland war in Scotland (Killiecrankie 1689) were anything but bloodless.
items.why: The 'Glorious Revolution' as bloodless English self-determination is a Whig myth. It was a foreign-backed coup with extensive bloodshed in Ireland and Scotland — successful, but not peaceful.

items.title: Lenin tried to remove Stalin from his deathbed
items.claim: In late 1922 and early 1923, Lenin dictated a 'Testament' commenting on his potential successors. What did it say about Stalin?

options.text: It praised Stalin as the most capable administrator and probable successor
It called Stalin 'too rude' and proposed removing him from his post as General Secretary
It did not mention Stalin at all
It endorsed Stalin only as a temporary compromise with Trotsky

items.reveal_title: Suppressed by the man it condemned
items.reveal:
In a postscript dictated on 4 January 1923, Lenin wrote: 'Stalin is too rude and this defect... becomes intolerable in a Secretary-General. That is why I suggest that the comrades think about a way of removing Stalin from that post.'

After Lenin's death in January 1924, the Testament was read at the Central Committee but suppressed. Stalin offered to resign at the 13th Congress; the offer was rejected and the document was buried. It was not published in the USSR until 1956 under Khrushchev.
items.why: Stalin's consolidation of power was not authorised by Lenin — it was achieved despite Lenin's explicit, dying objection. The myth of Stalin as Lenin's chosen heir was built later.

items.title: Elizabeth I owned around 80 wigs and 2,000 dresses
items.claim: Elizabeth I's image — the painted face, the wigs — was carefully constructed. How extensive was the wardrobe?

options.text: A handful of ceremonial robes for state occasions only
Inventories at her death (1603) recorded around 2,000 gowns and roughly 80 wigs, with ceruse make-up to mask smallpox scarring from 1562
She refused jewels and dressed plainly throughout her reign

items.reveal:
Elizabeth survived smallpox in October 1562 with scarring on her face and neck. She used ceruse (white lead and vinegar) to whiten her skin — slowly poisonous.

Nicholas Hilliard's 'Treatise Concerning the Arte of Limning' notes that after about 1590 painters were instructed not to show shadow on her face — the 'Mask of Youth' image. The wardrobe was a political instrument: gifts from courtiers carried specific meanings.
items.why: Elizabeth's reign was a sustained exercise in image management. The 'Gloriana' iconography was deliberate state branding, not personal vanity.
